question.problem:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{4}, & -1<x<3 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If $Y={(1-X)}^{2},$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
question.worked_solution:
First, notice that the transformation $Y={(1-X)}^{2}$ is two-to-one over the entire interval $-1<x<3.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14231916/assets/03718360bf910c74c22b36f34ad2f63bfad6d9387c0cdc62d3fb366a52f356c9.png)

Moreover, for $-1<x<3,$ we have that $Y$ is nonzero on $0\le y<4.$ 

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0\le y<4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({(1-X)}^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-{y}^{1/2}\le 1-X\le {y}^{1/2}) \\  & =P(-{y}^{1/2}-1\le -X\le {y}^{1/2}-1) \\  & =P(1-{y}^{1/2}\le X\le 1+{y}^{1/2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})-{F}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0\le y<4,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(1+{y}^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(1-{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}({f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2})).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}({f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}(\frac{1+{y}^{1/2}}{4}+\frac{1-{y}^{1/2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{y}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}, & 0\le y<4 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
